# **Your kids love video games. Which are the safest ones to play?**

![Sam Liberty](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fill:64:64/1*41-c96FhtKnOsntes5_iZQ.jpeg)

--

5

Listen

Share

A colleague of mine has kids in grade school and high school. She’s careful about digital wellness, sets screen time limits, does all the responsible parent things. We were having coffee a few weeks ago when she asked me point blank: “What games are actually safe for my kids to play?”

She’d been researching, reading parenting blogs, trying to make sense of it all. But every time she thought she had a handle on things, her kids would come home talking about a new game all their friends were playing. Roblox, Fortnite, something on their tablets. Were these okay? Should she say yes? Were there better options?

As someone who designs games for a living, I knew the answer was more complicated than she hoped. Because here’s what most parents don’t know: the video game industry has split into two camps. One designs games as entertainment. The other designs games as psychological manipulation engines built to extract money from your kids.

The frustrating part? Both look identical to parents who aren’t familiar with the space. Both are colorful, both claim to be fun, both are popular with kids.

So I created a flag system to help her evaluate any game her kids asked about. And because I’m guessing you’re in a similar position, I’m sharing it here.

## **The Safety Flag System**

Think of this like beach flags. Green means swim freely. Yellow means caution. Red means serious risks. Double red means stay out of the water.

### **✅ Green Flag Games**

### ⚠️ **Yellow Flag Games**

### 🚩 **Red Flag Games**

### 🚩🚩 **Double Red Flag Games**

Now let’s look at the games your kids are actually asking about.

## 🚩🚩 **Roblox**

I’m starting here because this is probably the game you’re most worried about. And you should be.

Roblox hits multiple double red criteria. Around 40% of users are under 13, and on the surface it looks innocent: a creative platform where kids build and play games, kind of like Minecraft.

![]()

But the safety record is alarming. The platform faces at least 35 lawsuits alleging that users meet and abuse children on the gaming platform or that it helps facilitate child sexual exploitation and grooming. ([ABC News](https://abcnews.go.com/GMA/Family/roblox-announces-new-safety-measure-amid-spate-lawsuits/story?id=127626071)) At least 30 people have been arrested since 2018 in the United States for abducting or sexually abusing children they had groomed on the platform. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_safety_on_Roblox))

The chat moderation has been particularly problematic. Users have been documented evading Roblox content and chat moderation to perform sexual content by taking activity offsite to other social media platforms, especially Discord, with applications showing that the large majority of users in these communities were under 15. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_safety_on_Roblox))

Roblox is finally implementing stronger measures. Starting in December 2024 in select markets and globally in January 2026, Roblox requires facial age verification or government ID to access chat features. ([Roblox](https://corp.roblox.com/newsroom/2025/11/roblox-requires-age-checks-limits-minor-and-adult-chat)) For children under 9, chat features are automatically turned off by default unless parents provide consent. ([ABC News](https://abcnews.go.com/GMA/Family/roblox-announces-new-safety-measure-amid-spate-lawsuits/story?id=127626071))

These are improvements. But they’re reactive fixes after years of documented problems, and they don’t address the user-generated content issues or the monetization model that encourages constant spending.

But even if the moderation in the game were perfect (it isn’t), the fundamental problem with Roblox is the exploitative business model. Yes, it’s “free” to play, but each game within Roblox sets its own costs, paid not in dollars and cents but in Robux, a digital currency that obscures the actual cost of purchases. On top of that, most games require users to convert Robux into the game’s own currency, adding yet another layer of obfuscation.

If I bought 10,000,000 gems for 1,350 Robux, how much is a gem worth in dollars? Nobody knows. And that’s the point.

**If your child already plays Roblox:** Disable chat entirely for kids under 13. Use maximum parental controls. Monitor which games they’re playing within Roblox (yes, games within the game). Have regular safety conversations about never sharing personal information or moving conversations to other platforms.

**My honest take:** The risk-to-benefit ratio doesn’t make sense when safer alternatives exist. This is the one game where I think parents should feel comfortable saying no, even if “all their friends play it.”

## **✅ Minecraft**

Here’s some good news: the game that’s almost as popular as Roblox is actually one of the safest options available.

Minecraft is a sandbox game where players mine resources, craft tools, and construct structures, offering endless creativity and serving as a platform where children can build virtually anything they imagine. ([ESRB](https://www.esrb.org/blog/what-parents-need-to-know-about-minecraft/)) As kids build and explore in Minecraft, they’re immersed in creative thinking, geometry, geology, and engineering, gaining experience designing and making something from start to finish. ([BrightCanary](https://www.brightcanary.io/minecraft-parental-controls/))

Teachers around the world use Minecraft in classrooms. There’s even a dedicated Education Edition designed specifically for learning.

![]()

What makes Minecraft particularly safe is how Microsoft designed the default settings. Microsoft designed Minecraft with child safety in mind, with default settings for young children automatically disabling chat and multiplayer features. ([Familyitguy](https://www.familyitguy.com/minecraft-safety-guide.html)) Parents can control multiplayer access, chat features, and friend lists through Microsoft account settings, giving substantial control over their child’s gameplay experience. ([Minecraft](https://www.minecraft.net/en-us/article/parental-controls))

You buy it once and that’s it. No constant monetization pressure, no aggressive FOMO tactics, no strangers in chat unless you specifically enable that.

**The one catch:** Kids can become obsessed and play for hours. The open-ended, creative nature makes it genuinely engaging (in the way Legos are engaging). But this is a time management issue, not a safety issue. Set clear boundaries about screen time and Minecraft becomes one of your best options.

**My recommendation:** Green light for ages 6 and up. For younger kids (under 10), keep them in single-player mode or set up a private realm where they only play with real-life friends. For older kids, you can gradually expand multiplayer privileges as they mature.

## ⚠️ **Fortnite**

Fortnite might surprise you. It’s probably safer than you think, but it still requires parental involvement.

Here’s what’s actually good about Fortnite: All microtransactions in Fortnite are purely cosmetic, with skins, emotes, and battle passes providing no competitive advantage. ([TekRevol](https://www.tekrevol.com/blogs/fortnite-revenue-usage-statistics/)) Your child won’t lose matches because they didn’t spend money. They won’t be at a disadvantage against kids whose parents buy them stuff. The game is genuinely free to play in full.

![]()

This is actually responsible design. Many game designers (including me) consider cosmetic-only monetization to be one of the more ethical approaches to free-to-play games.

The problem is how Fortnite sells those cosmetics. Seasonal refreshes with frequent updates and limited-time modes drive fear of missing out and purchases, with the average player spending $102 annually on cosmetics. ([TekRevol](https://www.tekrevol.com/blogs/fortnite-revenue-usage-statistics/)) Parents have sued Epic Games over limited-time sales creating a false sense of FOMO for younger players. ([PC Gamer](https://www.pcgamer.com/games/battle-royale/parents-are-suing-epic-over-fortnite-item-shop-fomo-timers-they-say-are-inaccurate-and-manipulative/))

Your kid will see a Spider-Man skin available for “24 hours only” and feel like they’re missing out if they don’t get it. They’ll see their friends with the current season’s battle pass skins and feel left behind. This is intentional design meant to create urgency and anxiety.

Fortnite also has voice chat in squad modes, which pushes it toward red flag territory. However, you can disable voice chat in the settings.

**My recommendation:** Ages 12 and up only, with firm boundaries. Set a strict spending limit (I’d suggest zero, or maybe $10/month maximum). Disable voice chat unless they’re playing with real-life friends they know from school.

Most importantly, use Fortnite as a teaching opportunity. Talk about why the game creates limited-time offers. Help your child recognize the manipulation. Ask questions like “Why do you think they only make this available for one day?” Kids are smart; once they understand they’re being manipulated, they often become more resistant to it.

For younger kids (under 12) who can’t yet critically analyze marketing tactics, I’d skip Fortnite entirely. They’re not ready for that level of psychological sophistication.

## 🚩 **/** 🚩🚩 **Free-To-Play Mobile and Tablet Games**

Now we get to the worst category: the casual games your kids download on their tablets and phones.

These are the games that show up in ads. The ones with bright colors and cute characters. The ones that look innocent but are actually designed with one primary goal: maximize revenue per user.

I can’t list every problematic game (there are thousands), but I can give you the warning signs:

![]()

### **Red flags:**

### **Double red flags:**

If a game has three or more red flags, delete it. If it has any double red flags, delete it immediately.

Let me give you a real example. My son accidentally subscribed to a “premium” coloring app that cost **$11 *per week***. He thought he was just trying out a new feature. The app was designed specifically to confuse kids about what they were signing up for. This is what we call a “dark pattern” in design: an interface deliberately created to lead users into choices they wouldn’t make if they understood what was happening.

These games use the same psychological techniques as casinos. Variable reward schedules. Artificial scarcity. Social pressure. Loss aversion. Except they’re targeting children who don’t have fully developed impulse control or the ability to recognize manipulation.

**My general rule:** If it’s free-to-play on mobile or tablet and popular with kids, assume it’s exploitative until proven otherwise. The exceptions are rare enough that this heuristic will serve you well.

## **✅ Nintendo Switch and Console Games**

Let me end with the best news: there’s an entire category of games designed with your child’s wellbeing in mind rather than your wallet.

Games like Super Mario, The Legend of Zelda, Mario Kart, and Kirby on the Nintendo Switch represent what I consider the gold standard of kids’ gaming. Nintendo has built robust parental controls into the Switch through a dedicated mobile app, allowing parents to monitor playtime, set daily limits, and restrict online features. ([Nintendo](https://www.nintendo.com/en-gb/News/2023/November/Nintendo-Switch-parental-controls-three-safety-tips-for-parents-2478405.html))

![]()

These games check every green flag box. You pay once (typically $40 to $60) and get the complete experience. No surprise charges. No psychological manipulation. No chat with strangers (most are local multiplayer only or have very limited online features). No energy systems or loot boxes or artificial scarcity.

When my son plays Mario Kart, he’s learning timing, spatial awareness, problem-solving, and how to handle both winning and losing gracefully. When he plays a typical free-to-play mobile game, he’s learning to navigate dark patterns designed by teams of behavioral psychologists.

The same goes for other console games on PlayStation and Xbox, though you’ll need to be more selective there since those platforms have a wider range of mature content. Stick to games rated E (Everyone) or E10+ (Everyone 10 and older) for younger kids.

**The catch:** The upfront cost. A Nintendo Switch costs around $300, and games are $40 to $60 each. The Switch 2 is even more expensive. For many families, this is a significant investment.

But here’s how I think about it: compare that $300 plus a few games to the “free” mobile games where kids can rack up hundreds of dollars in a few months of microtransactions. Or to Roblox where you’re paying in both money and risk. The Switch is actually the more economical option over time, plus it becomes a family activity rather than isolated screen time.

If the cost is prohibitive, consider buying used, looking for refurbished models, or even sharing a console among siblings or with another family.

## **What To Actually Do**

Okay, you’ve got the flag system and you know how the popular games stack up. Now what?

**When your child asks about a new game**, take five minutes to investigate:

**Set up systems, not rules.** Instead of arguing about each individual game, create a framework:

For younger kids (under 8): Primarily offline games or heavily supervised play. Minecraft in single-player mode. Nintendo games. No chat with anyone they don’t know in real life.

For older kids (8 to 12): Expand to carefully monitored multiplayer. Private Minecraft realms with friends. Maybe Fortnite with strict spending limits and disabled voice chat. Regular conversations about manipulation tactics.

For teens (13+): More freedom but maintained awareness. They’re old enough to learn about manipulative design. Use games as teaching opportunities: “Why do you think they designed it this way? What are they trying to make you feel?”

**Play with your kids.** Not just watching over their shoulder, but actually playing. You’ll understand what they’re experiencing, you’ll spot problems faster, and honestly, many of these games are more fun than you’d expect. Some of my best conversations with my kids have happened while building something together in Minecraft or competing in Mario Kart.

![]()

## **The Big Picture**

My colleague left that coffee conversation with a plan. She felt equipped to make decisions instead of just reacting to whatever her kids brought home next.

The video game industry isn’t going to fix this on its own (there’s too much money at stake), and regulatory efforts are slow. That leaves us parents to be the gatekeepers. It’s not being overprotective to say no to Roblox. It’s not being mean to set spending limits on Fortnite. It’s not being out of touch to delete exploitative mobile games.

You’re being exactly what your kids need, even if they don’t realize it yet.

So the next time your child asks for that game all their friends have, you’ll know exactly how to evaluate it. And more importantly, you’ll know you’re making an informed choice rather than just hoping for the best.

Your kids will thank you later. Even if right now they’re just annoyed you won’t let them download whatever showed up in a YouTube ad.
